synopsis: The booklet proposes staged intervention rather than an immediate full stop: information and warning progress to slowing, partial braking and maximum safe braking, with motion inhibit for a stationary machine whose projected path is obstructed [f13925, f6255]. Escalation gives the operator a chance to respond: sufficient operator deceleration stops the escalation, while shrinking stopping margin drives further intervention; transition to maximum braking should use remaining stopping margin and its uncertainty, not range alone [f13926, f13880, f11713, f6280]. Maximum safe braking is reserved for otherwise unavoidable collisions and remains constrained by stability and control limits; automatic slowing can be inadequate downhill, drivetrain response varies, and partial braking can conflict with following machines [f6268, f6262, f6263, f6267]. ISO 21815-3:2023 places intervention at collision-risk level 4 or above and permits prior warning, while South African law specifies detect, warn, retard to safe speed, then brake; ISO 21815-1 excludes automatic steering [f6201, f13939, f13936]. Mine leaders preferred slowing to a crawl before setting the brake, but accident data alone cannot establish whether full braking, staging, speed reduction or propulsion inhibit is appropriate for a particular machine and conditions [f3028, f3406]. Much of the relatively simple warn-then-brake logic can be designed and checked at model-in-the-loop level in late 2026 before sensor selection, with stage-specific acceptance tolerances and virtual tuning informed by measured brake delays and deceleration maps [f13332, f13942, f14054].
